name: West Engelheim
description:
West Engelheim is what happens when a neighborhood is abandoned by every institution designed to sustain it and then has the audacity to survive anyway. The original West Englewood was already one of Chicago's most disinvested communities before the Consolidation — decades of redlining, capital flight, and political neglect had hollowed it out block by block. When the corponations drew their sovereignty maps, they drew around West Englewood the way water flows around a stone. Nobody wanted it. Nobody claimed it. It became one of the purest jurisdiction gaps in GLMZ — a place where no corporate flag flies because no corporation saw profit in planting one.

The vacancy is the defining feature. Entire blocks stand empty — not ruined, exactly, but vacant in a way that feels intentional, as if the buildings are holding their breath. The bungalows and two-flats that once housed families are now structural shells, their interiors stripped for salvage, their facades still standing like stage sets for a play nobody is performing. Between them, the lots have gone feral — not with nature, because the soil is too contaminated for much to grow, but with improvised structures, tent communities, and the particular architecture of people building shelter from whatever is available. The community-led revitalization efforts that characterized pre-Consolidation West Englewood have evolved into something harder and more autonomous: a self-governing zone that operates on reputation, mutual obligation, and the understanding that no help is coming from above.

The Lot Councils are the closest thing to governance. Organized block by block, each council manages its territory with a combination of democratic process and pragmatic authority. They allocate salvage rights, mediate disputes, coordinate defense against incursions from adjacent gang territories, and maintain the community gardens that provide a surprising percentage of the district's nutrition. The gardens are West Engelheim's quiet miracle — hydroponic rigs built from salvaged medical equipment, soil remediation projects using engineered mycelia, rooftop plots that produce actual vegetables in a district the city classified as a food desert thirty years ago and never reclassified.

There is a fierce pride here that outsiders often mistake for hostility. West Engelheim does not want your charity. It does not want your development proposals. It does not want to be someone's reclamation project. It has already reclaimed itself, thank you, and it did it without a single corporate grant or municipal permit. The cost of that independence is visible in every jury-rigged power line and every child who has never seen a licensed medical professional. But the alternative — surrendering autonomy to whatever corp decides the land is finally worth taking — is not something the Lot Councils are willing to consider. Not yet. Not ever, if they can help it.

sights: Vacant bungalow facades standing in rows like monuments to a previous city
Community gardens glowing under improvised grow-lights on rooftops and in converted lots
Lot Council meeting fires visible at dusk — circles of people making decisions by firelight
Salvage crews moving through empty buildings with the methodical efficiency of archaeologists
Children's murals on vacant walls — bright colors insisting on presence in a place designed for absence
Improvised power lines strung between buildings like a nervous system made of copper and hope
sounds: Wind through vacant structures — a hollow, fluting sound unique to empty buildings
Lot Council debates carrying across open lots in the evening air
Hydroponic pumps humming in converted basements
Salvage tools — pry bars, cutting torches, the percussion of careful demolition
Guard dogs — real ones, not drones — barking at the perimeter of claimed blocks
smells: Growing things — soil, greenery, the particular scent of hydroponic nutrient solution
Contaminated soil — a faint chemical undertone that never fully dissipates
Welding and metalwork from salvage processing operations
atmosphere.feel: Defiant in a way that is quiet rather than performative. West Engelheim does not advertise its resilience. It simply continues to exist, which in GLMZ is its own form of resistance. There is warmth here, but it is the warmth of people who have learned that warmth must be generated internally because nothing external is coming.

demographics: Predominantly African American, reflecting the pre-Consolidation demographics, with a growing population of displaced residents from adjacent districts pushed out by corporate expansion. Almost entirely untier-ed or Tier 1. Population is estimated at 15,000-20,000, though the Lot Councils keep their own census and do not share it.
economy: Salvage is the primary economy — stripping vacant buildings for reusable materials and selling to buyers in the Circuit and adjacent districts. Community gardens produce food for local consumption and limited trade. Skilled labor — welding, electrical, construction — is traded between blocks on a favor economy. There is no corporate presence and no formal currency circulation.
power_structure: The Lot Councils govern block by block through consensus process. A rotating Inter-Council Assembly meets monthly to address district-wide issues. No single leader, by design — West Engelheim learned from watching other neighborhoods get decapitated when their leadership was co-opted or eliminated. Defense is organized by a volunteer patrol called the Watchers, who are respected but deliberately kept from accumulating political authority.
dangers: No emergency services of any kind — medical emergencies are handled by community medics with limited supplies
Contaminated soil in many lots — long-term health effects are a slow crisis
Incursions from gang territories to the east testing the Watchers' perimeter
Corporate land speculators sending scouts to assess property values — a prelude to forced acquisition
Structural collapse in vacant buildings that have not been properly assessed
Total absence from official infrastructure — no grid power, no water service, no waste management
opportunities: A jurisdiction gap this clean is valuable to anyone who needs to operate without corporate oversight
The Lot Councils are pragmatic — they will work with outsiders who bring genuine value and respect the process
Salvage rights can be negotiated for specific buildings if you have something worth trading
The community gardens represent genuine agricultural innovation — the mycelia soil remediation technique has applications elsewhere
Safe harbor for people running from corporate jurisdiction, if the Watchers vouch for them
story_hooks: A corporate survey drone was shot down over West Engelheim. The Lot Councils found the drone's data cache and discovered detailed property valuations for every block in the district. Someone is preparing an acquisition play, and the councils need to know who before the legal machinery starts moving.

One of the community medics has been treating patients with symptoms consistent with a new soil contaminant — something that was not in the ground six months ago. The contamination pattern suggests deliberate introduction, possibly to trigger a health emergency that would justify forced evacuation.

A Watcher patrol found a body in a vacant building — someone from the Spire, based on the augmentation quality. No identification, no neural ID broadcast. Someone very high-tier died in West Engelheim, and someone will come looking.
frequented_by: Lot Council members and community organizers
Circuit buyers looking for salvaged components
